sentences.text: Coelophysis was a bipedal, carnivorous theropod dinosaur that was a fast and agile runner.
Gregory S. Paul estimated the weight of this gracile form at 15 kg, though later estimates reached 25 kg for a robust variant.
The species possessed a furcula, which is the earliest known example of this bone in a dinosaur.
Its hand featured four digits, with only three being functional and the fourth embedded in the flesh.
The type species Coelophysis bauri was described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1889.
Excavations at Ghost Ranch revealed a fossil layer containing hundreds of Coelophysis skeletons in a single concentration.
Excavations at the Ghost Ranch Coelophysis quarry continued through 1947 and 1948 by the American Museum of Natural History crew.
The Ghost Ranch quarry was reopened and worked between 1981 and 1982, yielding 16 large blocks weighing between 6 and 10 short tons each.
All material from Ghost Ranch was described by Colbert as belonging to a single species of Coelophysis known from hundreds of individuals.
Rinehart et al. concluded in 2004 that Coelophysis was a diurnal, vision-oriented predator based on a complete scleral ring found in a juvenile specimen.
Its eyes appear most similar to those of eagles and hawks, with high accommodation power.
The tail had an unusual structure in the prezygapophyseal joints forming a semi-rigid lattice, seemingly allowing movement only up and down.
This tail structure may have acted as a rudder or counterweight to help the animal maneuver at high speeds.
Megapnosaurus was once considered a species of Coelophysis, but it is now recognized as a valid separate genus.
In 1999, Sullivan and Lucas named the specimen NMMNH P-22298 and material previously assigned to C. willistoni as Eucoelophysis after AMNH 7224 was designated the neotype of Coelophysis bauri.
It lived during the late Triassic and early Jurassic, approximately 203 to 196 million years ago, in North America and Africa.
Coelophysis fossils from Ghost Ranch were found in the upper sandstone level of the Chinle Formation, which was believed to be Norian in age at the time of discovery.

According to the stratigraphy proposed by Sullivan, Lucas, and colleagues, Coelophysis lived in the Revueltian-age Petrified Forest Formation while Rioarribasaurus lived in the Apachean-age Rock Point Formation.
It is debated whether scattered fossil material found worldwide in Late Triassic and Early Jurassic formations belongs to Coelophysis or similar animals.
While Colbert considered Coelophysis diagnostic, Richard Padian argued it was a 'metataxon' lacking unique characteristics due to its scrappy and incomplete original material.
It is debated whether additional theropod material can be referred to Coelophysis, as Richard Padian argued the type material was too incomplete to justify such referrals.
Material from relocated sites was used to argue that Coelophysis is distinct from Rioarribasaurus based on differences in the pubis, femur, and metatarsals.
Hunt and Lucas believed that none of the material from three species possessed unique characteristics supporting their synonymy with C. bauri or other theropods.
In 1993, paleoartist Gregory S. Paul opined that Coelophysis was indeterminate and that Rioarribasaurus and Syntarsus belonged to the same genus, proposing the combination Syntarsus colberti.
